passages.text: At dawn Peter went out and stood at his usual place for discussion, where he saw a large crowd assembled. Just as he was about to speak, one of his attendants came in and said, ‘Simon has arrived from Antioch. Having learned as early as last evening that you had promised to give a discourse on sole sovereignty, he is ready, together with Athenodorus the Epicurean, to come upon you while you speak and publicly oppose everything you say in any way in support of sole sovereignty.’ While the attendant was saying this, look—Simon himself was coming in with Athenodorus and some other companions. Before Peter could say anything, Simon spoke first:

lexical_decisions.chosen: on sole sovereignty
lexical_decisions.rationale: The discussion concerns the rule of the one God, not a particular human monarchy. Sole sovereignty retains the political-rule image without replacing it everywhere by the broader modern term monotheism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of his attendants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes one who serves Peter. An ecclesiastical deacon is possible, but a formal office is not established by this occurrence alone.

passages.text: ‘I learned that yesterday you promised Faustus to demonstrate today, presenting your discourse in order and beginning with the Master of all himself, that he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods, and that whoever acts otherwise must be punished eternally. Above all, I am truly astounded at your recklessness in hoping to persuade a wise man, an old man at that, to your own wishes. But you will not achieve your designs, especially with me present here to expose your false arguments. Perhaps, had I not been present, the wise old man would have been deceived, since he is unfamiliar with the books publicly credited among the Jews. For now I will pass over lengthy arguments so as to expose your promise more quickly. Therefore begin to say what you promised in our own presence, for we know the scriptures. If, however, ashamed of exposure, you wish to pass over your promise in our presence, that too is sufficient proof that you are lying, because you did not dare to speak before those who know the scriptures. And why am I now waiting for you to speak, when I have the greatest witness to your promise in the old man standing here?’ Having said this, he looked directly at our father and said, ‘Tell me, most honored of all men, did not this man promise to demonstrate to you today that there is one God, that one should not call or consider anyone else a god, and that whoever acts otherwise, as someone sinning most grievously, must be punished eternally? Or will you not answer me?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν μόνον δεῖ λέγειν, ἄλλους δὲ μήτε λέγειν μήτε νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: God is the understood predicate supplied by the discourse and explicitly repeated later in the same passage. Both calling and regarding are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δημοσίᾳ πεπιστωμένων βίβλων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the books publicly credited among the Jews
lexical_decisions.rationale: The books' accepted authority is attributed to the Jewish community in Simon's speech. Credited or held trustworthy is the sense, not a claim that their contents have already been proved in this debate.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You would rightly demand testimony from me, Simon, if Peter had first denied it. As things stand, I will not be ashamed to say what needs saying. I think you want to debate while cut through by anger, which is unfitting for you to do and for us to listen to. It means witnessing a quarrel, not being helped toward truth. Knowing from Greek education how inquirers should proceed, I will now remind you. Let each of you set out his own doctrine, and let your arguments be directed against the other. If Peter alone sets out his view while you keep yours silent, an argument you put forward might press against both his view and yours. Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated: the one who set out his view would, but the equal defeat of the one who did not set out his view would not be evident. He might even be thought to have won.’ Simon answered, ‘I will do as you say, but I fear that, having already been won over by his words, you will not be a truth-loving judge.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: cut through by anger
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle preserves the image of being cut or sawn through. The main text does not substitute a fire image; sawn through by anger is a more specific lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ εἰς ἕτερον οἱ λόγοι γενέσθωσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and let your arguments be directed against the other
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reciprocal contrast of two speakers supports each directing argument toward the other. It does not require appointing an unnamed third interlocutor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἀμφοτέρους ὑμᾶς ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἡττηθέντας μὴ φαίνεσθαι ἡττημένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The next clauses specify that only the openly stated position would visibly lose. Both actual defeat and asymmetric appearance are retained, without changing the hidden position into a victorious one.

passages.text: Our father answered, ‘Do not force me to agree with you without judgment so that I may seem a truth-loving judge. If you wish to hear the truth, I am more predisposed toward your view.’ Simon said, ‘How are you predisposed when you do not know what I think?’ Our father said, ‘That is easy to know; listen to how. You promised to expose Peter as lying when he says there is one God. It is entirely clear that someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood does not, if he speaks truly, say the same thing. For if he says the same thing as the one speaking falsely, he too is lying. But if he demonstrates the opposite, then he speaks truly. You cannot, then, call the man who says there is one God a liar unless you believe there are many gods. I too say there are many gods. Since I agree with you before the inquiry, I am more predisposed toward you. In this respect you have no need to be anxious about me; Peter does, since I still think the opposite of him. After your inquiry, I hope, as a truth-loving judge who has stripped off preconception, to agree with the prevailing argument.’ When our father had said this, a subdued cry of praise arose from the crowds because he had argued in this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one speaking falsely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the participle in a middle sense concerning false speech, since the conditional argument compares two speakers making the same supposedly false assertion. A material passive alternative is the one being falsely accused or lied about. That passive sense does not itself establish the accused person as actually false; neither reading is presented as uncontested, and the conditional remains hypothetical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who has stripped off preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clothing-removal image and the need to set aside a prior opinion are both retained, rather than changing the father's initial shared belief into an already completed conversion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τὸν ἕνα λέγοντα ψεύσματος ἐλέξαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied print has ἐλέξαι. Convict follows the context, especially the preceding explicit ἐλέγξειν and the charge of falsehood, rather than treating the form as choosing a speaker. Normalization to ἐλέγξαι would be a proposed Greek change, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected print is claimed.

passages.text: And Peter likewise said, ‘I am ready to do as the mediator of our discussion has said, and now, without any further delay, I will set out my view about God. I too say that there is one God, who made heaven, earth, and everything in them. It is not permitted to call or consider anyone else a god.’ Simon said, ‘But I say that the scriptures trusted among the Jews speak of many gods, and that God is not angry at this, because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: the mediator of our discussion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The role concerns moderation of the exchange, not a theological mediator between God and humanity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτὸν διὰ τῶν γραφῶν αὐτοῦ πολλοὺς θεοὺς εἰρηκέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine subject and possessive scriptures are retained as Simon's stated reason. They do not represent an independent translator's conclusion about scriptural authorship or polytheism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And Peter likewise said
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected print reads ὁμῶς, ordinarily alike or likewise, and that sense is preserved. It does not itself mean the adversative nevertheless normally spelled ὅμως; no accentual normalization has been supplied. Likewise concerns Peter's joining the exchange and does not assert that his doctrine agrees with the father's preceding many-gods view.

source_issues.source_quote: ἄλλον. δὲ οὔτε λέγειν οὔτε νομίζειν ἔξεστιν.
source_issues.issue: The selected print places a full stop after ἄλλον before δὲ. The English treats the surviving words as one intelligible construction. This is disclosed punctuation treatment, not a lacuna, a supply of missing words, or an allegation that a corrected Greek print has been verified.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods themselves also brought this before us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

lexical_decisions.chosen: themselves also brought this before us, saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed form is treated as a form of παράγω, bringing forward or passing by. The main text preserves its presentation sense, with this pointing to the following quotation. A material intransitive alternative is passed before us, saying. The quoted prohibition functions as instruction, but that function is not substituted for the movement or presentation verb; no Greek correction is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: firmament
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves say that there are many gods and at other times that there is only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

lexical_decisions.chosen: what must we conclude
lexical_decisions.rationale: The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: mislead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. The makers appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: you shall surely know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tempter was testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated testing root is retained, with tempter distinguishing the agent from God in Peter's stated argument. The noun is not silently replaced by a personal name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: angels have been called gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves the pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving that attachment silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.

passages.text: ‘Besides, it belongs to the Father not to have been begotten, but to the Son to have been begotten. What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten.’ Simon said, ‘Even if it is not the same in respect of generation?’ Peter said, ‘One who is not in every respect the same as another cannot have all the same designations as that one.’ Simon said, ‘That is assertion, not demonstration.’ Peter said, ‘Why do you not understand that the one is self-begotten or even unbegotten, whereas the other, being begotten, cannot be called the same, not even if the begotten one is of the same substance as the begetter .... But learn this too: human bodies have immortal souls clothed in God's breath. Having come forth from God, they are of the same substance, but are not gods. If they are gods, then by that reasoning the souls of all humans—those who have died, those living, and those yet to be born—are gods. But if, persisting in your argument with me, you say that they too are gods, what great distinction remains even for the Messiah in being called God? For he has what everyone also has.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γεννητὸν δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ ἢ καὶ αὐτογεννήτῳ οὐ συγκρίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three generation terms and their distinctions are retained. Self-begotten is not silently collapsed into unbegotten, and the comparison is not rewritten to assert a later creedal formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ καὶ τῇ γενέσει οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστιν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if it is not the same in respect of generation?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes εἰ καί concessively in response to the preceding distinction and preserves οὐ as actual nonidentity. A material alternative interprets the utterance as a negative question seeking assent: Is it not the same even in respect of generation? That alternative remains a negative question, not an affirmative conditional. Generation can mean coming-to-be or birth and is not silently replaced by substance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of the same substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is retained both in the conditional argument about the begotten one and the subsequent account of souls. The passage's own distinction between shared substance and the title God is not harmonized with another theological position.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in being called God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied dative form occurs in the title-ascription expression. The English preserves the intended naming construction without supplying a further predicate or claiming to correct the printed Greek.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints four dots after the begetter clause. The English preserves exactly four dots, without supplying a missing verb or continuation. Its rendering of is in the preceding conditional clause provides ordinary English copular syntax and does not claim to restore the unavailable wording after the clause.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Surely “God,” which everyone says, is not his unutterable name, that you insist so strongly even about the name, so that it may not be given to another?’ Peter said, ‘I know that this is not his unutterable name, but the one spoken by human convention. If you give this to another, you will attach the unspoken one to another too. In terms of intention, the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one. On this account the insult is reckoned also against what has not yet been spoken, just as honor directed toward what is known is referred to what is not yet known.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: unutterable name
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can denote a name not to be divulged or spoken. Secret name is another possible emphasis; the subsequent spoken/unspoken contrast supports unutterable without specifying the hidden name's letters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ λεγόμενον ὄνομα τοῦ μὴ λεγομένου πρόοδός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Advance toward reads the movement from the public designation to the unspoken name, because the preceding conditional traces giving the spoken name to another into consequently attaching the unspoken name to another. A materially different genitive reading is the spoken name is a going-forth of the unspoken one, or its outward expression, in which the movement originates in the unspoken name. Both directions are disclosed; the main text is contextual rather than a claim that the genitive uniquely means toward. No hidden name or magical utterance is supplied.

passages.text: ‘See, Simon, what kind of God you wish to persuade us to be ungrateful toward! The earth still carries you, perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do. For you were the first to dare what no one had dared, the first to utter what we heard for the first time. We were the first and only ones to witness God's boundless patience in the face of such impiety from you—not that of some other god, but of the one who created the world, against whom you dared to be impious. No chasms opened in the earth, no fire was sent down from heaven or advanced to burn people, no rain was withheld, no multitude of wild beasts was sent from the thickets, and God's destructive wrath did not begin even against us because of one sinner, as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh. For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth? For even now, most grievously blasphemed, he would have inflicted the greatest punishment. But, on the contrary, he is patient and calls us to reorientation toward God. He has destructive arrows stored in his treasuries for the destruction of the impious, which he will release like living creatures when he takes his seat to repay his enemies with judgment. Therefore let us fear the righteous God whose form the human body bears as an honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴσως δὲ ἰδεῖν βουλομένῃ τίς σοι τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν τολμήσοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle is read as continuing the personified earth, despite its oblique inflection beside the nominative earth. Perhaps qualifies the conjecture; the English does not replace the earth with an unexpressed masculine observer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ τότε ἐπεξελθὼν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς κτίστης θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed negative question is retained rather than turned into a categorical identification or categorical denial. Its relation to the following counterfactual punishment and contrasting patience is rhetorically difficult. A reading that challenges the attribution of the earlier punishments to the creator is materially possible; the main text preserves the question rather than deleting the negative or resolving the theology by emendation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calls us to reorientation toward God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied English policy uses reorientation for moral-spiritual redirection, with toward God where the context supports the destination. Here the creator's invitation contrasts with the preceding impiety against him; us is the contextually inferred addressee, not a claim that God himself must reorient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συντελοῦντα βέλη πρὸς συντέλειαν τῶν ἀσεβῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: destructive arrows ... for the destruction of the impious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated completion or ending root describes final, destructive force. The English retains the destructive aim and the arrows image without supplying a specific weapon technology.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like living creatures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The life-bearing comparison is explicit; it does not say that the arrows are literally a named species of animal or angel.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐπὶ μοιχείας πνευματικῆς τῆς κατὰ σάρκα χείρονος ὑπαρχούσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main reading takes adultery according to the flesh as the genitive of comparison and attaches worse being to spiritual adultery. It is favored by the surrounding rebuke, which presents Simon's impiety as especially serious. A material alternative takes adultery according to the flesh as subject of a genitive absolute: adultery according to the flesh being worse. That reverses the comparison and is not excluded by morphology alone. This is a disclosed attachment ambiguity, not an unverified printing defect.
